--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.reverse()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Reverse the direction of all edges in the graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.reverse()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Reverse the direction of all edges in the graph. title: >- [Graph.reverse()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Reverse the direction of all edges in the graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Reverse the direction of all edges in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L49764-L49892){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.reverse() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Reverse edges](../assets/graphs/reverse.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed graph on A, B, C, D with arrows A to B, B to C, D to C, and A to D. After reverse(), the same four edges point the opposite way, B to A, C to B, C to D, and D to A, all drawn in the accent color." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with the same nodes but all edge directions reversed (`u->v` becomes `v->u`). For undirected graphs, returns a new copy (no structural change). Preserves all node and edge attributes. The reversed graph (also called the transpose) swaps the roles of "in" and "out": a node's in-neighbors become its out-neighbors, sources become sinks, and everything a node can reach becomes everything that can reach it. That makes it useful for: - asking "who can reach this node?" with forward-only tools such as BFS or descendants - flipping the meaning of a relation (e.g., "provides" into "depends on", or "cites" into "is cited by") - algorithms that need the transpose, such as Kosaraju's strongly connected components Node and edge IDs, labels, weights, and attributes are carried over unchanged (each edge keeps its ID, just pointing the other way). The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph with reversed edge directions (same directedness as the original). ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~ancestors`) : The nodes that can reach a node, without reversing. [](`~descendants`) : The nodes a node can reach. [](`~pagerank`) : A ranking that follows edges forward. [](`~to_undirected`) : Drop the direction of every edge. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Reversing a directed path flips each edge, while the original keeps its own: ::: {#c0fe4508 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec original = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")], directed=True) flipped = original.reverse() ( original.has_edge("A", "B"), flipped.has_edge("B", "A"), flipped.has_edge("A", "B"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, True, False) ``` ::: ::: Weights and other edge attributes travel with their edges, so the reversed edge "B -> A" keeps the weight `4.0` of the original "A -> B": ::: {#13cd47b7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighted = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B", 4.0)], directed=True) weighted.reverse().get_edge_df().select("source", "target", "weight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Cited by, instead of cites In a citation network each edge runs from a paper to an older paper it cites, so the arrows point back in time. Reversed, each edge runs from a paper to a newer one that cites it, and the arrows follow ideas forward. Moreau 2000 cites nothing, but is cited by 9 papers, and 14 build on it directly or through other papers: ::: {#d4a8b70f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} citations = ec.citations() cited_by = citations.reverse() direct = cited_by.get_successors("Moreau 2000") indirect = cited_by.descendants("Moreau 2000") len(direct), len(indirect) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (9, 14) ``` ::: ::: Any method that follows edges forward now runs the other way. PageRank on the citations finds the work everything rests on, with Moreau 2000 on top. On the reversed graph, rank flows to the papers that cite the most, and it collects at Osei 2021, which cites the survey Hughes 2020, which cites 11 papers: ::: {#c10f0c86 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def top(graph): scores = graph.pagerank(return_dict=True) return graph.get_label_from_id(max(scores, key=scores.get)) top(citations), top(cited_by) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ('Moreau 2000', 'Osei 2021') ``` ::: ::: The papers are drawn as a timeline, oldest on the left, and sized by PageRank, with the citations first and the reversed graph second. The largest node moves from Moreau 2000, at the far left, to Osei 2021, at the far right: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#676cd7ec .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} citations.pagerank().plot( layout="pos", size_by="pagerank", color_by="field", show_labels=False, width=360, height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
